message.reasoning_content:
I'm faction 0. Current president is faction 1. Round 5 action. If I bribe 5 to player 1, I get influence 3 > their 2, becoming president in law — but law entry happens after action, so influence counts then. Being president gives veto power and the 5% commission tiebreak. But bribing player 1 also enriches them (cash rival). Bribing player 2 also raises influence without boosting the richest rival... wait player 1 has 26.6M, I have 23.5M. Bribing player 2 (4.9M cash, 2 goods) keeps me closer in rank.

Actually influence matters for: presidency (veto + 5% commission if max influence). Bribing 5M to idx2 gives me influence 3, max influence → 5% of bank (1.9M) plus presidency control. Cost 5M, but I lose 5M cash to a rival anyway. Bank is 38M, 5% ≈ 1.9M. Presidency lets me veto bad laws in rounds 5 and 6.

Alternatively produce goods for next market (round 6 sell). Goods=2 worth ~2×8=16M at market. That's actually valuable. Hmm, round 6 market: counter at 2, prices 9,8. Selling 2 units ≈ 17M. Produce gives 2 goods → 17M revenue vs bribe cost 5M for 1.9M commission + veto control.

Veto value: law could tax 20% or nullify promissory — I hold 27.5M promissory! Card 8 zeroes promissory; I could veto it. That's crucial. Also cards 1/2 tax future sales.

Best: bribe 5M to player 2 (poorest, less cash threat) → influence 3, become president, protect promissory. But bribing enriches them; fine. Also produce gives goods for last market worth ~16M... can't do both.

Wait bribe costs 5M, produce gives ~16M revenue. But presidency protects 27.5M promissory which is only realized as cash at start of round 6. Card 8 would zero it — worth veto. But wait, would others vote yes on card 8? Others have no promissory; yes they'd vote yes. Card 8 could come in round 5 law. So presidency veto is critical to save 27.5M. Cost 5M. Choose bribe 5M to 2 (choice 11) — or to 1 (choice 4)? Player 1 is closest cash rival at 26.6M; giving them 5M makes them 31.6M, far ahead of me. Player 2 at 4.9M + 5M = 9.9M. Give to 2.
